This seems like an example of Simpson's paradox, where the direction of the association between the treatment and success rate reverses when accounting for a third variable, in this case, stone size. 

Wait, Simpson's paradox occurs when a variable that is confounding the effect (hidden variable) is not considered. Here, the stone size is a confounder. Even though Treatment B has a higher overall success rate, when you control for stone size, Treatment A is better in both categories. But because Treatment B was applied more to the category (small stones) where it performed worse relative to A, its overall success rate appears higher.
